utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you tell, please, when you were first retained by lawyers to appear in this case?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was around July 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before or after, on your recollection, either Dr. Donia or Dr. Allcock had given evidence?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall when Dr. Donia gave evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before or after Allcock gave evidence?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was before Dr. Allcock gave evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So that the allegations you make about Dr. Allcock were available to the Defence lawyers to put to him if they chose to?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because my report was not completed or in progress at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was it drafted?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The section on Dr. Allcock was most certainly not drafted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Had you been invited by the lawyers to comment on Dr. Allcock's report?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And your comments were thus available to the Defence lawyers?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And may we assume arising from consistency that they would have been broadly in line with the nature of your allegations against him in your report?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, what would have been broadly in line?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, your comments on Dr. Allcock's report would have been broadly in line with the allegations you now make against him?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's hard to say. At that time, I was not as thoroughly engrossed in the empirical studies by Dusko Sekulic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But in general, at the very least, Mr. Kordic's lawyers at that time, I think it was Mr. Stein, were in a position to raise with Dr. Allcock the various criticisms you now make?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, if you told them about it, they were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think it's probably a matter of comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Because you as a sociologist would accept, wouldn't you, that there are a range of competing theories on many, if not most topics?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And the only fair way to deal with these matters is for competing theories to be thrashed out by competing theorists?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would put it to be empirically verified.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's just, therefore, -- it would probably be easier, you would accept, for a Tribunal dealing with the issues raised by these various reports simply to hear from the various experts rather than have it all filtered by lawyers. It would probably be easier that way, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't understand that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll move on. Your report contains a passage dealing with your curriculum vitae, to which I will return, and then just to remind the Judges, if they don't have it before them, it contains a huge number of appendices and to which I'm not going to go into them in detail at all, but I just want to identify them. Appendix A1 simply sets out the various plans for partition and reorganisation and cantonisation of Bosnia-Herzegovina; correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In Appendix A2, you list mini wars and civil -- it must be wars that raged within, you say, Bosnia-Herzegovina, even as Croats and Muslims fought as an alliance. You remember that?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm going by recollection, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So you are acknowledging internal warfare not just a matter of the Serbs attacking, things like that?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm saying one could characterise this as several conflicts going on simultaneously.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Appendix A3 is headed, "Competing interpretations and the chaos of concepts." Can you just tell me what that -- what part that has to play in your report?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't have the report in front of me, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, you can have it, of course. You had the marked one yesterday, you can have it today.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think I can go by memory. It is simply to state that there are, indeed, many different interpretations upon what happened in Bosnia-Herzegovina and that the ones offered by the Prosecution's expert witnesses are two among many.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What was the purpose of your report, as you understood it, you were providing? What was its purpose?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was first of all to rebut the expert testimonies of Drs. Allcock and Donia; and then second, to offer an alternative explanation of what occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: To rebut -- I'll come to the specific purpose of rebuttal in a minute, but just help me with this before I move on. Was the tone of your report your own decision or was that suggested to you by the lawyers?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean by "tone"?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, the tone of your report could hardly be stronger. You accuse people of bias, you try and link the experts with the Prosecution. Was that all your idea?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I see. We then come to appendix A4, which is an interview with Muhamed Filipovic.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The significance of that? Just trying to get somebody else's evidence in, or what's its significance?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Its significance is that because Dr. Donia puts so much emphasis on the Karadjordjevo meeting, that Dr. Filipovic, who was very close to President Izetbegovic, reports that he and Mr. Zulfikarpasic made forays for negotiation, cantonisation, reorganisation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, around the same time as Karadjordjevo, with the Belgrade regime. So the point of that is that there were many competing plans for the reorganisation of Bosnia-Herzegovina going on at roughly the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, either witness statements or summaries of witness statements -- that takes us through appendix A5 as well, which is Adil Zulfikarpasic's statement, and I'm not going to deal with those. Likewise, A6 is Sefer Halilovic, another account of somebody else who fell out with Izetbegovic; yes?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not quite. I think that given that General Halilovic was the Chief of Staff of the Bosnian army, that his account is something worthwhile here to take note of, and it basically puts into context the other actors in this drama. Whereas, as I've noted in my report, Drs. Donia and Allcock tended to focus primarily on President Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Again, in the absence of the witness being here, we can't weigh him, and I shan't deal with him. Appendix B, Huntington's view on the cultural East/West divide. Just explain, please, so that I can understand that. What's the significance of that?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both of your expert witnesses take Franjo Tudjman's 1981 book on contemporary nationalism in Europe and treat it as some sort of blueprint or some sort of relationship to the events that occurred during this tragic war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the purpose was to show that Franjo Tudjman makes historical comments that are very similar to what an eminent Harvard historian -- namely, Samuel Huntington -- says about the general deterioration of Islamic Western relations in the post-Cold War world.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The mere fact that Huntington may be, in your terms, eminent, says nothing about the underlying purposes or intentions of Tudjman, does it?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Tudjman's intentions are a matter for the Court to decide. I was referring very clearly to historical writings.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Akbar Ahmed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like to know what is the relationship between Dr. Tudjman and the well-known Croatian historian and Samuel Huntington, the author of the famous book called "Clash of Civilisation." Would you please try to explain to me, because I don't really understand what is the link between them.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is the question being posed to me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is no, that I know of, direct or personal link between them. What I was trying to say was that President Tudjman's writings, as a historian, in his 1981 book do bear some resemblance on this issue of there being an East/West clash with those of Professor Huntington, and that therefore the way that Dr. Donia and Dr. Allcock take some of the statements out of context in Mr. Tudjman's book to suggest intent on the partition of Bosnia-Herzegovina seems to me to be an arbitrary conclusion. So that I'm, by bringing in Samuel Huntington, simply widening the context and saying historians, intellectuals write and discuss about these matters without there necessarily being any sort of a blueprint for war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but I think that this comparison is rather daring, because we have a book which is written by a historian, who at the same time is a man of action, on a particular situation which concerns the future of a people, of a nation; and on the other hand, there is a very general conjecture post-Cold War, and the end of ideologies and the conflict, the confrontation between civilisations. I do not really think that there is anything in common between them. Are we talking about a man who is a historian, at the same time a man of action, such as Mr. Tudjman? We are not now discussing an academician or an academic or a man of learning, a professor.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, at the time Franjo Tudjman wrote that book, he was a professor. He was not a man of action. He became a man of action and a politician after he had been imprisoned and following the elections in 1990. So that I am making a comparison, a contrast, strictly on the basis of what Mr. Tudjman wrote before he became a man of action.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Appendix C, Akbar Ahmed. Significance, please.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Akbar Ahmed is a distinguished anthropologist at Cambridge University who also writes about a general world-wide clash between Islam and the West. Moreover, he believes that this very general clash, which he sees going on from Kashmir to Palestine to Bosnia, to Chechnya, and other places, is the result, actually, of a vacuum in Western leadership. And I think again it offers an interesting contrast, which is what a scholar should do, in examining, as I did examine the works of Dr. Allcock and Dr. Donia, to present competing, opposing, different points of view and explanations for the phenomenon being considered here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This particular expert's field of expertise is where? It's the Indian subcontinent, isn't it? You're not suggesting, are you, that his works in some way excuse or justify the actions of individual politicians or soldiers in the Balkans?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, and I don't see where you would get such a conjecture. He is an expert on the South Asian continent, but he's also a distinguished anthropologist who has written many books on many topics, and certainly his book "Living Islam" pertains to Islam all over the world and was a BBC televised series.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Appendix D was public opinion studies -- I'm probably going too fast, I'll try and slow down -- was public opinion studies in Croatia as against the rest of Europe. I'm not going to deal with those. We don't have the raw material with us. Appendix E was empirical research conducted by Lazic and his team on the status of ethnic minorities and inter-ethnic relations in Croatia. Would you accept that that fits with and isn't in contradiction with what Dr. Allcock says?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry. You said fits with and contradicts? I don't understand that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I didn't say "in contradiction."

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At least, I hope I didn't. It fits with and supports what Dr. Allcock says, is what I intended, whatever I said.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He does not cite that study. There's no way for me to determine.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do its findings fit with and support what he says or do they contradict them? Because if they contradict them, let me know exactly how and then I might be able to deal with it. Otherwise I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think I made it clear yesterday, it's very hard to find a clear statement in Dr. Allcock's testimony because he cites so few scholars. He does not cite the study.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll come to that point immediately rather than later. Citation is one thing, clear statement is another. Dr. Allcock's statements are entirely clear, aren't they, about what you take exception to in such strong and sometimes virulent language. You understand what he's saying.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I disagree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, we'll have a look at some passages later. As to citation, Dr. Allcock was instructed, as he makes clear, to provide a general background to assist the Court, not necessarily a learned study. Do you really make complaint of the lack of citation?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I have already stated, when one looks at some of his claims, it's really difficult to know what he's saying because he does not cite. I can give you a very specific example, if you'd like.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, give it.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, on page 32 of his report, if you have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, we can find it, that's not a problem.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I need a copy in front of me, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That can be provided by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There was a problem in your page numbering, sorry -- it was not in his -- I'll come back to that later.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, if you look at seven, Roman numeral six, he writes, "Expressions of social distance".

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could it be placed on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Somebody asked to put it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Put it on the ELMO, could you? Yes, can we have the relevant part?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Only one part. "Expressions of social distance are notably sensitive to changes in political climate. Two studies done in 1985 and 1990, for example, found that in that period the degree of closure or distance manifested by Albanians had grown remarkably." Now, the problem here is Albanians could refer to the actual Albanian minority which is very small in Yugoslavia, or to the Albanian people in Albania, or to the Kosovo Albanians but then again, it doesn't say where. One has to assume that these are the same studies that I have spoken about by Lazic and by Sekulic, but it is not at all clear. But even then, what's most problematic here, as I stated yesterday very clearly, in 1985 and 1990 the point of comparison is Croatia. These studies were not done on Kosovar Albanians or any Albanians in 1985 so this is, in fact, a misleading statement. It does not cite, and as a colleague, as a reader, as anyone, one has to make guesses as to what it's true intention is. So this is what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As to that example, you were quite right --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You are quite right about the studies he was basing it on.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not clear. One has to guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, they are dealt with in your Appendix E, aren't they, where you indeed do make the appropriate guess because you deal with Lazic's research and you say, 'implies but doesn't cite' this study of Dr. Allcock?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I wouldn't think one had to guess in circumstances such as these. I mean as a professor, as an editor of books, I'm used to things that when somebody makes an argument to present very clearly what they are saying, why, and who they are drawing upon.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If he'd cross-examined on this complaint then the matter could have been clarified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's not a matter for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Appendix F is the empirical research conducted by Dusko Sekulic and I have no observations to make on that at all. Appendix G is USIA surveys and again in the absence of raw material, we can't deal with that. Appendix H is the 30-page, 31-page rebuttal of John Allcock's testimony which wasn't put to him and so I can't and won't deal with that in detail. Appendix J is the 10-side or 9-side rebuttal of Robert Donia's testimony and again, that not being explored with him I am not going to deal with that. And then we have Appendix K, Senator Daniel Patrick Moynihan on the self-determination versus the sovereignty of nation. Can you just explain that, please?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, along the lines of Professor Akbar Ahmed, who is saying in the post-Cold War world, there is a general tendency towards scission, towards chaos, because the world seems to have been thrown out of control. So to speak, Senator Moynihan wrote a book called "Pandemonium" to that effect and, again, I think it was an interesting alternative and an interesting contrast to the focus of your expert witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Providing what answer so far as the Balkans is concerned, so that I can understand it?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So far as what is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So far as the Balkans are concerned and this particular war, what is the answer that it provides?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Similar to the answer I gave to one of the Justices yesterday, that precisely because the International Community was disorganised at the time the war erupted in the former Yugoslavia, that gave rise to people falling back on nationalism as a fall-back position.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, does that in any way legitimise any specific activity in Yugoslavia, Patrick Moynihan's theory?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And then is it finally, I think, we have Tudjman's theory of nationalism and what's the significance of that?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, for the sake of scholarly completeness. Since that book is used by your expert witnesses, I think it should be noted simply for context. This is a book about nationalism throughout Europe, not about Bosnia-Herzegovina, not just about the former Yugoslavia. When one analyses a text, one generally notes the general context. So he was concerned with the rise of nationalism and how this problem could be dealt with throughout Europe.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Again, does it legitimise anything specifically?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I offer it for the sake of context.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. Let's come back to your curriculum vitae, and one thing isn't clear to me. You cover a very wide area geographically. Indeed you cover the world geographically, in your studies and writings.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sociology is a cosmopolitan enterprise. I suppose I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's not clear, from what you set out, the degree, if any, to which you engage in field work; do you?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I engaged in the field work in the field of mental health and I had some publications on that, but I am primarily a theorist.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, you are a general, abstract theorist; correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what a general, abstract theorist means. I apply social theory to interpret studies and events. That's what theorists do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And you are wholly dependent on the field work of others in the sociology works -- in the sociology works that you engage in?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would be careful with the word "dependent". I analyse, put into context, criticise the work of others.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You are also, well, you accept that, of course, Dr. Allcock has been visiting Yugoslavia and engaging in field work there for 20 years or more?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that for a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But you have no reason to doubt it?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. You make obvious points about the performance of scholarship. I think indeed in your bibliography you cite some 400 works. Are they all cited in the text?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is that padding of a bibliography, please?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As I state in my report, I wish to set a fuller context. It's not padding, I've made it very clear to show that there are a plethora of views and opinions and competing interpretations of what occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What was your Ph.D. dissertation in, please?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "In the shadow of Plato: Durkheim and Freud on Suicide and Society".

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did that have any connection with the particular topic at hand?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Better explain it.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the dissertation deals with not only suicide, with murder, accident rates, death and destruction; how these things relate to the development of societies; how we can use social theory to explain these things as social facts, and I think these kinds of investigations actually are connected to the kinds of issues that are coming to the foreground here in relation to this war.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You got a Fulbright scholarship. Of course you will recognise another fellow Fulbright scholar, Bill Tomljanovich, sitting behind me, won't you? Another Croat of American nationality on the same scholarship; yes?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll come back to that a little later. Can I now look, please, at some of the comments there have been on your work in various learned journals and I'm going to end, you will be interested to know, with comments by Dr. Allcock on your work. Have you read them?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to his review of my book "Balkanisation of the West"?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I may have read it a while ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And what we will discover so far as he is concerned is that he takes an even-handed approach to you, he's not -- well, we'll look at in its course. Your Honour, these come in bundles, I hope. They don't, I'm sorry they have to be dealt with separately, but I want them to be before the Court. 1465.8 because there aren't many of them. If we could have the next one ready to go as soon as the first one is distributed. John Armitage's criticism on the barbarian temperament and the whole thing is in context and this is one view of an academic on you. Right hand column, just over half way down the page, "A final criticism," if one can see that. "A final criticism concerns the sheer scale of Mestrovic's ambitions. Thus he claims he not only wants to complete Horheimer's affinities with Schopenhauer, but also to supply what he calls a depth sociology and psychology to the works of Baudrillard, as well as subverting the traditional view of both Durkheim and Freud. This is something of a tall order, to say the least. Still, if critical theory's reach does not exceed its grasp, what's a post-modern philosophy for?" Would that be some of the reflection of the criticism for you that you try and encompass far too much --

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if it's general, I think for me the interesting line is it's a provocative and timely contribution to post-modern critical theory; that's merely all an author would like to see, that's basically a favorable point of view.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next one please, 1472.9. This is on the first sheet, we see under the line where it says "Garth Massey, University of Wyoming": "The prolific professor Mestrovic has added another volume to his list of recent publications, this time combining his revitalization of Durkheim's theory of primacy of morality with a partisan interpretation of the war in the former Yugoslavia, all in the light of 'the affinities between post-modern narcissism and post-communist violence'. It is a daunting and original effort that earlier admirers of Stjepan Mestrovic's work will enjoy. Readers new to his writing may be put off by some intemperate language and a point of view that eschews neutrality." If you turn to the next sheet, the first column, last complete paragraph, the judgement on you here by a fellow academic: "The books central thesis a marred by chapters that may be expected to elaborate, but tend to detract from, Mestrovic's formulation. Chapter 2 is devoted to dismantling the link between Croatia and Nazism and hanging the label of 'Nazis' on Serbia. Chapter 4 applies a superficial post-modernist framework to dissect and critique the U.S. media presentation of the war in the former Yugoslavia, including coverage of wide-scale rape of non-Serbian women." Do those comments reflect some of the judgement of you that you are -- that you eschew neutrality?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think it's a general trend. Again, I think this is a favourable review. Calling me prolific and saying I make some significant contributions to this is all an author can hope for.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 1465.6, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Nice speak a bit more slowly when he cites.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, we are asked to speak a little bit slowly when you read the citations.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I've been alerted, and I'll do my best to keep on favourable terms with the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This, then, by Jan Kubik, and if we look to the last sheet -- I think this is "Habits of the Heart," isn't it?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That should be Thomas Cushman.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thomas Cushman. Thank you. Yes. I want to come back to that in detail later, for a particular reason. But what is said here in the second sheet and in the second column, where you're dealt with in this way, or your book is dealt with in this way: "There are a number of potential problems with an ambitious and broad theoretical study of this kind, not the least of which is paucity of any data on the relationship that the author suggests among family dynamics, religious culture and the emerging structure. At the same time, glaring contradictions to his theory are ignored, such as male-centred Islamic culture that also produces 'virulent' nationalism." And then about ten lines further down: "Most importantly, 'cultural' studies that draw directly on theories of individual behaviour to explain larger social phenomena oversimplify the link between the two levels of analysis. If 'normal' nationalism is defined by public support of the state by the nation, for instance, when did the duly elected Nazi government cross the line into 'virulent' nationalism? By skipping over the interceding structural processes and social dynamics that translate individual action into larger social institutions, his methodology forgoes the stuff of sociology and is limited to blanket explanations that cannot explain social change. Moreover, such a methodology risks promulgating social stereotypes, one of which could be the unregenerate chauvinism of eastern European males." Is that a sort of typical criticism that there has been of your work, or works, with Cushman?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not a work with Cushman, first of all. And second, your reviewer takes a pejorative view of Islam here. And I'm very glad I did not make the claim that she attributes to me, because I find it pejorative. And given that she does have a pejorative view towards Islamic males and eastern European males, no, I don't find this particularly troubling.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, now, what I'm going to do, because the time taken to deal with this is time that is in short supply, is I'm going to leave out several which I may try and lay before the Chamber in another way more succinctly later. But I think it's only fair that you should see the Allcock review, which is 2826. You told us yesterday you've never, I think, heard of --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You told us yesterday you've never heard of Dr. Allcock, but it appears you may have heard of him in relation to the review of your books.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I came across the review when I began the project, my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I see. Well, this relates to "Balkanisation of the West", and of course was written entirely independently of any known involvement of you in this case or independent of this case altogether. On the second sheet, page 575, towards the bottom -- well, perhaps it's worth looking at the end of the top paragraph. Would you agree with this description of yourself, about eight lines town: "Mestrovic is never a man to pull his punches, even though some of them turn out to be wild swings rather than crisply executed upper-cuts. Consequently, his work is always dramatically thought-provoking, although that experience may result in disagreement with him." Then towards the bottom of the page, about -- a couple of inches up, about 20 lines up: "Mestrovic is obviously unaware of the huge disparity which has grown up between popular and governmental responses to the situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Consequently, he moves from observations about the inadequacy of politicians, and especially American politicians, to a diagnosis of the total moral depravity of the West, which seems to me to go beyond what the evidence will support, bearing in mind the fact that one of his motivating concerns is a rediscovery of the social and cultural conditions which support caritas. Perhaps he should have devoted a little more attention to the phenomenon of a massive upwelling of popular sympathy for Bosnia among the ordinary people of Europe." And then two lines up from the bottom of the page: "While taking seriously Mestrovic's insistence upon the importance of cultural continuity, however, we do need to be careful about the dangers of overgeneralisation." Then the next page, please. "It seems to me to be a perfectly respectable and prima facie convincing hypothesis that the collapse of communist rule will not result in a sudden cultural transformation of the countries of eastern Europe but will reveal the strength of cultural traditions older than communism which in many respects are equally as infertile a soil for the growth of democracy. Where Mestrovic does his own case a disservice, however, is in his apparent readiness to conflate the cultural history of all formerly communist states to a lowest common denominator. This intermittently takes the form of appeals to the work of Dinko Tomasic, which, whatever its merits or demerits, does not provide conceptual seven-league boots which permit Mestrovic to move from the hypothesised cultural attributes of Dinaric man to all Balkan peoples, and thence to the cultural substratum of all communist countries." And then a comment by the author, which I can pass over, unless it's wanted to be read. But the last paragraph: "If neither post-modernism nor post-communism will bear close conceptual examination, what are we left with? This is a fascinating book. Every colleague I know who has read it has been gripped by its interest. Their response, as well as my own, derives as much from the desire which it rouses to debate the issues which Mestrovic raises rather than simply to adopt his analysis. He also offers us a confluence of three important endeavours: a deep engagement with the social and cultural development of the South Slav peoples, driven by a realisation that this is more than parochial interest; a passionate concern for moral truth; and a keen interest in the value of theory." Here is somebody who disagrees with you, as you can see, strongly, and can do so courteously. Do you still think that the tone of your report was appropriate in this case?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am courteous when I disagree with colleagues. And by the way, this is a very flattering review and I appreciate it. I am very courteous with colleagues when I disagree with them in meetings of the American Sociological Association, learned societies, and so forth. I did not see the task here as anything personal in Dr. Allcock. He made some claims in his expert report which I found wanting, I cited some empirical studies that I think contradict it, and that's that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And you think it right, do you, to suggest, as we can find in your report on several occasions, do you think it right to suggest that these experts, Dr. Donia and Dr. Allcock, may, as it were, be fitting in with the Prosecution's case? Is that what you're suggesting from time to time?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fitting in the sense that the arguments you make and the arguments they make fit the general pattern of top down, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You're not suggesting, are you, or are you, there's been any changing of opinion by these two men, neither of whom comes from the former Yugoslavia and each of whom just has a long interest in the country -- you're not suggesting that either of these men has tailored a view to fit the Prosecution, are you?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I may come back to reviews a little later, but before I do, can we look, please, at just one passage, page 2 of your report. There's a slight difficulty with your report in that the page numbers are repeated, but the body of the report is clear. So if we can look at just one passage in detail --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness have a copy of his report.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Page 2. It can go on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And it's towards -- it's just a little over -- it's about six lines down on the second paragraph: "Most sociologists accept Weber's central argument ..." The interpreters I think have copies of this document. It's on page 2 and six lines down on the second paragraph. "Most sociologists accept Weber's central argument that highly rational ends/means behaviour, including capitalism, science, rational music and arts, among other cultural products, is possible and is enshrined in Western countries with a predominantly Protestant, especially Calvinist cultural base; namely, the USA, Canada, Great Britain, the Netherlands, and Germany. Countries and societies with non-Protestant cultural bases, ranging from the former Soviet Union and the former Yugoslavia to India, tend to lag behind in cultural activities that regard rational demand, rational ends/means behaviour. Even if this finding is offensive to cultural groups that seek to emulate those that enshrine rational ends/means behaviour, it has been replicated on numerous occasions across the world. It must be emphasised that this sociological argument is cultural in that it involves learned behaviour and does not make any racial or biological assumptions of any sort. Also, sociologists do not make an inherent association between rationality and values," and so on. Now, that passage, would you accept that that would be regarded as offensive to, for example, Croats or Croats living elsewhere in this world?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Does it not suggest inferiority?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think it states very clearly that I'm not making a value judgement about rationality; simply that rationality does refer to organised, systematic ends/means behaviour, which is indeed taken for granted in the West and is not so prevalent in other countries. For example, there are more lawyers per capita in the United States than anywhere else in the world. Lawyers deal with what is known, and they bury in terms, as rational legal authority. There are much fewer lawyers in non-Western societies. Issues that in the West would go before a court would be settled there by more traditional sources of authority. In no way am I saying that the West is superior; I'm saying the West is different, and there are studies in sociology that document this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At one place in your report I haven't immediately to hand, but we can find it, you even suggest that catching a bus or going to a restaurant, I think, is a qualitatively different experience in the Balkans from that which it is in the West, that that is somehow culturally driven and a reflection of fundamental differences. It's on page 2, I think -- page 3.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think if anyone has had an experience of going into a restaurant in eastern Europe, I think it's a fairly general one -- there may be some exceptions, but in general it's a very long wait to get served and to move out, whereas in the United States there is a huge emphasis on fast-food restaurants, such as McDonald's, Burger King, and so forth, which are highly efficient, which are highly organised, and again I think exemplify, not in my view, but in the views of sociologists such as George Ritzer, who take this varying view, do exemplify some of these principles.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm going to suggest to you that the proposition you advance is extreme and extended, and unpalatable to people who can produce mathematicians, who can run trains on time just as well as people in the West. But you won't accept that?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because again I've cited for you George Ritzer's book on the subject, and no one finds it, to the best of my knowledge, unpalatable; in fact, it's very popular. It is standard reading in most sociology courses in the United States. There are many, many conceptualisations of the United States being a sort of fast-food kind of place. I don't think this should be construed as offensive in a culture that does not take to fast food.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, have you ordered a meal recently in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I was going to make that point, Your Honour, but I thought that, out of respect for my host country, I shouldn't make it publicly. But, Your Honour, I entirely agree with the underlying thesis. May the witness please have a copy of Dr. Allcock's report. I don't know if there's a marked copy in the Defence bench. Is there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's right here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you lay on the ELMO appendix 6. This is an appendix that I think you did not comment on in your report, presumably because you had nothing to say about it. It's right at the end. If you bring it here, I'll find it. Let me lay this one on the ELMO. Here it is. You understand that at the time that Dr. Allcock prepared his report, he had and could have had no knowledge that you were involved at all in the work of the defence for Kordic, so that his appendix 6 was written ignorant of your future involvement. And we'll just read it. It's a page and a half, and I'll ask for your comments. He says he heads it with your name and the theory of social character and he says this: "The political transformation of Croatia and the Croatian national movement in general has gone along with several attempts on the part of academics of different disciplines to provide intellectual foundations for secession from Yugoslavia. These are of interest and relevance to this report for three reasons: One, they support the claim that Croat secessionism has been more than an ad hoc and pragmatic response to the course of the political and economic crisis which engulfed the federation after 1989. Two, these ideas were being advanced in some case by individuals who were close to the leadership of the HDZ. Three, while not necessarily indicating that their authors held to views which could be described as racist are open, in some cases, to a reading along that line and to exploitation by those who might wish to find academic justification for extreme political views." Now, you didn't comment on this appendix in your report unless I have missed it. If I have, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you accept his thesis?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tell us what's wrong with it then.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I made clear in "Habits of the Balkan Heart", I've following a trajectory or tradition established by writers such as Emil Durkheim, Alexis De Tocqueville, David Riesman in a book entitled "The Lonely Crowd" where he discussions the social character of Americans in a book that sold 1.5 million copies and David Riesman was my major professor at Harvard University. Seymour Martin Lipset who wrote a book called "Continental Divide" in which he argues that there are differences between social character between Canadians and Americans despite similarities between these peoples overall in language in religion, in ethnic mix, and in other factors. So it is a respectable, venerable concept used by people who in no way are racist and does not carry any connotations that would imply biology or that this character is indelible. It simply talks about what it is about a Canadian that makes him or her a Canadian versus an American. So, for example, Lipset talks about how Canadians tend to be conservative, tend to accept big government, whereas Americans tend to be very individualistic and they mistrust big government. In "Habits of the Balkan Heart", I'm doing no more or no less in suggesting something similar. That there is this idea of social character, something that makes cultural groups different.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What we've reached in this appendix of Dr. Allcock, if you look at it carefully, says while the authors -- well, not necessarily indicating that the authors held to views that could be described as racist, "... it's open to a reading along that line and to exploitation." Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's his opinion. I've never seen it used by anyone for racist points of view.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: He goes on to say this in paragraph two, "Young Croatian sociologist, Stjepan Mestrovic, has produced a succession of publications since 1993 in which he has sought to revive the work Tomasic. Tomasic issued in 1948 his personality and culture in eastern European politics in which he argued that the peoples of the Balkan region would be divided into two broad types, ethnographically speaking, the Zadruga culture and Dinaric culture. These were founded on different types of ecology yielding contrasting ways of life, different types of life which he believed gave rise to opposed personality types. His argument was that the history of the Balkan region in particular, but also eastern Europe more generally, could be understood in terms of cycles of conflict between these antithetical cultures. Tomasic interpreted the history of the Balkans in terms of cycles in which the war-like Dinaric pastoralists periodically descended from the hills to impose themselves upon the peaceful agrarian Zadruga agriculturalists. Following victory, they settled in towns, became assimilated by the lowlanders and embarked on a process of decadence to be replaced before long with another wave of Dinaric conquest." Now that is a summary but is that a summary of the Dinaric culture upon which you rely to explain these events?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What's wrong with it then?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dinko Tomasic was educated at the Sorbonne. He was a distinguished professor of sociology at Indiana University. He was highly respected in sociology. His book, which is cited, was favorably reviewed, and I cite those reviews in my book, in the American Journal of Sociology and a number of other eminent work. Basically what that theory states is again something that's nonproblematic. That in mountainous regions throughout the world, not only in the former Yugoslavia, there is a tendency to less cosmopolitanism, more isolationalism, less contact with other peoples. This is in true as the Appalachians in the United States, for example, as it would be in the hills of the former Yugoslavia. And that this isolationism, this lack of cosmopolitanism, coupled with the patriarchy of the way, usually the way the people are raised there, can produce a value system not an unchangeable one, not a permanent one that is not add odds and a cosmopolitan and more democratic outlook than one will find in a cosmopolitan urban setting in which people from many ethnic groups are thrust upon the other. That would be my summary of the significance of Dinko Tomasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And have I understood your report correctly, and I'm not sure that you are differing from Dr. Allcock, but that it's the mountainous Serbs that are more capable of top down calculated leadership and the lowland Croats who aren't; is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you will find that nowhere my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How does Dinaric culture as opposed to Zadruga culture have any bearing, please, on the unravelling by this Court of what happened in the Lasva Valley?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I did not bring this theory into the report. I did not bring this in to try to explain the unravelling of the Lasva Valley. I brought it in "Habits of the Balkan Heart", as I've stated in a larger discussion of De Tocqueville, Riesman, Lipset and other people in the disintegration of Yugoslavia following the end of communism. These are very different tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's just look at the last two paragraphs of what, ignorant of your future involvement, Dr. Allcock said. Paragraph three, just over the page, please, usher. "Although largely discredited since the period of its publication, the work of Tomasic has been taken up in the form of Stjepan Mestrovic's theory of social character as providing the basis for an interpretation of the events surrounding the collapse of Yugoslavia. Mestrovic goes beyond Tomasic in a number of respects particularly in that he quickly abandons the relatively firm ecological footing of the latter's ideas and frequently falls into a simple equation between Dinaric peoples and Serbs or Montenegrins and Zadruga types and Croats which borders on straightforward racism. (It happens also to be anthropological nonsense for a variety of reasons which it would be distracting to enumerate here.) An important point to note about the work of Mestrovic is that it is acknowledged by the author to be based upon his cooperation with Slaven Letica who was not only a sociologist based at Zagreb University but also an aide to President Tudjman. Together with the work of Anto Valenta, it does suggest that quasi-academic ideas which lend themselves to the support of ethnic intolerance have circulated regularly, and have been taken seriously, among those who hold influential positions within the HDZ both in Croatia and in Bosnia and Herzegovina." I take it you don't accept any of that.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Save for the fact that it's true that you were working in cooperation with Slaven Letica?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What do you say then, please, about the value of Anto Valenta's book?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I return to Slaven Letica for a moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's my friend's, he is my colleague. What is not noted is that he resigned for working for President Tudjman and has been one of President Tudjman's more severe critics. So this attempt to smear him and to smear me, again, in an unsubstantiated way. I notice here that there is no citation for my book, and I will repeat here again; in my book, I make it very clear I'm making a cultural argument, not a biological one, no ties to politics, and that I'm working in a very venerable tradition not relying upon Dinko Tomasic but putting him in the context of Alexis De Tocqueville's "Democracy in America," David Riesman's "The Lonely Crowd" and other venerable books. Now as for Anto Valenta, I have no connection, I don't know why Mr. -- Dr. Allcock would choose to link the work of Anto Valenta. In my book, I see no connection here whatsoever. I never cite him. I never knew about him. I see no connection here whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mestrovic, could we usually call you in sociology is called a "culturalist"?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, thank you. Do you draw some consequences about cultural differences are they based on the respect or lack of respect for human rights?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If Your Honour is asking me in general, yes, I do. In this report, I do not. If you care for me to elaborate in general in response to your specific request, I will do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Does this mean that the cultural diversity may justify the lack of respect for the human personality in certain cultures?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. What I would say, which I think would be supported by most cultural theorists, by most sociologists, is that the West does have an ingrained cultural tradition of respect for human rights, again, going back to the Declaration of Independence, the Constitution, the Bill of Rights, the Reformation, the Renaissance, a number of writings. There is a very long cultural and very rich cultural history in the West. I do not see it as offensive but I do see it as a matter of fact that those societies which did not experience those events, namely the Reformation, the Renaissance, the Bill of Rights and so forth will have a more difficult time, culturally, with the notion of human rights and therefore will have to, in a sense, experience it vicariously through the West.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And my last question about your views about nationalism in relation to the end of the Cold War. Mr. Mestrovic, do you think that a nationalist will ever come up, will invent a foreign enemy in order to be able to structure himself? Would you support that theory that a nationalist needs to create a foreign enemy in order to structure himself as a nationalist, in order to lend strength to his nationalism?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not necessarily, Your Honour. Instead, I would say that there are different varieties of nationalism. A certain amount of nationalism has to be present even in western societies or people would not go off to war. They would not want their children to die for a patriotic cause. They would not pay taxes. So that nationalism is tempered by other institutions in the culture which promote human rights and individualism. In other cultures, the nationalism, if it is not mitigated or tempered by other cultural factors, may degenerate into a war-like stance but again there will be mitigating factors.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the -- does nationalism need a foreign enemy or not?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not necessarily, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Nice, and of course I'm speaking in my own name, but I believe that we have made a round of theoretical and sociological views of Mr. Mestrovic and what interests us more specifically is his report insofar as it does with the case before us, so could you please try to focus on these matters? I believe that the Chamber has been amply informed today because you have before you professional judges and we are broadly informed about Mr. Mestrovic's positions as a sociologist.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, and my next topic was to pick up an answer of the witness to ask him this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You say that the purpose of your report was to offer, amongst other things, you said this, was to offer alternatives to the reports of Donia -- well, in particular, of Dr. Allcock. But what is your alternative? What have you provided?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's set in my report that the lion's share of the blame for what occurred in Bosnia-Herzegovina lies with Slobodan Milosevic of Serbia. It was Serbian aggression against Croatia first, and Bosnia-Herzegovina second, which created a set of circumstances, especially demographic conditions, which basically put tremendous pressure upon two peoples; the Bosnian Muslims and the Croats who, by the empirical research that I have cited, were extremely tolerant at the time. So a very tolerant Bosnia-Herzegovina was squeezed first by the fact that about 70 per cent of its territories went over to the Serbs about two weeks after hostilities started, and then the Bosnian Muslims and the Bosnian Croats, who were allies, tragically ended up fighting each other for an ever-decreasing share of the pie. That is the alternative explanation in summary form that I give.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Returning to His Honour's question just a minute ago, about the need or necessity for an enemy. The existence of an enemy creates a fertile territory, intellectual territory for the generation of nationalism and for the generation of ethnic intolerance, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not recognise that as a sociological theory. I would give alternatives to what you give.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I wasn't suggesting it as a sociological theory, I was asking it as a matter of common sense. If you have an enemy to fight that gives rise to the potential to build nationalism, it also gives rise to the potential to build ethnic disquiet particularly if -- well, go and answer that if you will, please.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't know what the term "common sense" means, I would rather stick to my sociological expertise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, you know what common sense means. Yes. Just answer the question, please.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe that intolerance does not necessarily lead to violence, and tolerance does not necessarily prevent war. I do believe that the enemy is created. It is not something that's waiting out there, it is created through a set of contingent circumstances and changes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is that any different from what Dr. Allcock has proposed?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Although I want to stay contemporaneous for the time being and probably for the rest of my questions which I hope won't go on much longer, there's one matter broadly connected that I'd like to go through with you. If you'd go to page 26 of your report, please. Now, on page 26 of your report, you -- bottom of the page, please. You make this suggestion, "Whereas the Prosecution uses the 'frame' of the Ustasha as the central focus for its depiction for the origins of Croatian independence in the 1990s, Sekulic uses the larger frame and so on." Now, where do you get that suggestion that the Prosecution used the frame of the Ustasha as the central focus for independence of the origins of Croatian independence?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Allcock's report goes into great length about the NDH, about Croatian iconography from that period, about Croatian symbols, and does make the suggestion that there were some connections between the HDZ and the symbolism of the Ustasha.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Shall we look, then, please, at Dr. Allcock's report, which we can lay on the ELMO conveniently. First of all, page 60. And we need only look at three short passages, but take us wider if you think the context demands it. Starting at page 60, in paragraph 3.4, the last few lines of which are what I refer to, what he actually says, having summarised some of the matters that you're referring to, but we can read in detail if we need to: "Not all Croat emigres were Ustasha supporters by any means. The Croatian Peasant Party continued to operate from headquarters in Canada." That's perhaps not such an important passage. If we go over to the next page, page 61, paragraph 4.1, this may be the passage you have in mind: "It is important to acknowledge the cautious and partial rehabilitation of the NDH, which the HDZ was prepared to support. Its position went by no means far enough for several more strident factions, notably the HSP. In some respects, the HDZ can be said to have adopted the superficial trappings of the NDH without committing itself publicly to its substance. Although the HDZ never advocated the extreme racist policies of the NDH, its concern to reiterate at every opportunity the narrative of the historical continuity of Croatian political identity led it to adopt historical symbols of the former Croatia, notably the checkerboard flag." To take matters fairly, and I hope swiftly, if we go to 4.2, where other matters, and in particular the renaming of streets in Zagreb, has been covered, Dr. Allcock says this at the end of 4.2, in brackets: "This practice has been given exaggerated importance on occasions in that the authorities have been criticised for including individuals who, while prominent in public life, were not necessarily supporters of Pavelic. However ill-informed criticism has been on occasions, its policy was controversial." And then finally on page 62, to see how Dr. Allcock really expressed the position, in paragraph 4.5, this, the last four lines, please: "Nevertheless, it is certainly not the case that the HDZ has espoused the racist policies and genocidal practices of that regime, and individuals who have done so have generally found their political home in other more extreme organisations within Croatia, such as the HSP." Now, that's actually how Dr. Allcock expressed himself. If we go back to what you were saying on your page 26, I'll just remind you, the suggestion that the Prosecution frame of the Ustasha as the central focus for the origins of independence is simply incorrect, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so, because there's a long and tedious discussion of the Ustasha and its symbolism in the Allcock report. It is central to, despite his many nuances and ramifications, to the discussion. And the context of my paragraph is clearly, if you read that page, in relation to Dusko Sekslic, who is making the point that there were eminent Croats who were instrumental in the creation of a multiethnic Yugoslavia. He never mentions that. And I think again, for the sake of context, I thought it was important to offer a contrast and a competing point of view.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I notice the time. I intend to reduce to the bare minimum what remains, and I hope it won't be very much longer. I imagine the other witness is available for this afternoon and certainly can be completed in the afternoon. I observe through this witness that the complaints made about or comments made about Dr. Donia and Dr. Allcock were never put to them, and indeed if I were to complete what I have to say in half an hour, it would always be possible for them to give their own explanations as they're here, should the Court want it, in answer to the complaints that are made, and we would be happy for that to happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll consider that. We'll adjourn for half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your top-down/bottom-up theory approach, if -- and this is going to be for the Judges, of course, to decide -- if it's found in due course that in December 1991 President Tudjman was planning for possible annexation of Bosnia and, further, was planning to keep things private by having a dual-track approach, doing something in public and doing something in private, if that's the case, that doesn't fit with your theory, does it?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If it's the case in January of 1992, at a meeting in Busovaca, Dario Kordic and others were speaking, and one in particular, a man called Kostroman, was espousing strong and, by many, thought to be unacceptable views on linkage with Croatia -- this is in January 1992 -- would that fit with your understanding of the history? This would be an HDZ meeting.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't understand the question. I mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's difficult not seeing the video, but we don't have time. If we have a political meeting -- I'm not going to trouble you too much with what Dario Kordic said, but just to take -- the man Kostroman, was saying that Busovaca was Croatian land and would be subject to Croatian laws. If that was a position being taken by representatives of the party in January 1992, publicly, so to whip up enthusiasm, does that fit with your theory of an absence of top-down control?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'd have to know the context.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. Yes. He was the secretary of the HDZ, the man Kostroman. Did you know anything about him?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Am I right in thinking you know nothing of the man Valenta, or is it that you don't wish to be associated with Valenta's works?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know nothing of the man Valenta.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we look at your report, please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I wanted to ask Dr. Mestrovic a question in relation to the top-down and bottom-up theory. Might it not be the case that what happened reflected characteristics of both top down and bottom up, or is it that the discipline that you pursue doesn't allow for that kind of mixture?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think Your Honour I would agree with you I think it does allow for a top down and bottom up, and it does allow for that kind of mixture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we look, please, at page 61 of your report following on the same topic. So if we just look at this, the end of the first paragraph, six, seven, eight lines up and I'll read it slowly. "The rational top down explanation may apply to Belgrade to some extent, but not to Zagreb and not to Sarajevo." Pausing there, should we, in light of your last answer to His Honour Judge Robinson say "but only to a limited extent" or "only to some extent to Zagreb"?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you explain how you never made that concession, really, in your report before?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I was responding to the rather one-sided approaches of top down that I found in the works of your expert witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. First of all, it's not accepted for one minute that that's the correct characterization of their reports or anything like it, but even if it were the case, do you have to respond to white with black if the true answer is grey?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are a number of places in this report where I make it clear that to some extent, either one of these or both explanations can be at work.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We may have to find those places. We may not have time. I press on. I read on, "The Bosnian Serbs supported by Belgrade, fought against the Muslim-led Sarajevo government forces and those of the Bosnian Croats. The two allies, Bosnian Croats and Bosnian Muslims, turned against each other for a time even as they remained allies during the same time in other parts of Bosnia. It cannot be repeated often enough that in the northern strip of Bosnia, especially, in Orasje, Bosnian Croat and Muslim brigades maintained their alliance against a common Serb enemy." The position, I think, is this: This is the Posavina you're talking about here, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Which is the strip of land that crossed the top of Bosnia providing an essential corridor so far as the Serbs judged it; correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And if one looks at, and Your Honour to save time I can lay on the ELMO my page of 92.1 which is a document we looked at yesterday, the Graz agreement, this is the agreement made at Graz and it's -- I want your help on these things, please. We see this, one and two items. One and two reveal disagreement or failure to agree between Serbia and Croatia in respect of Mostar. One says, "In the city of Mostar, the Serbian side considers the Neretva River to be the borderline, while the Croatian side considers the entire city of Mostar to be within the Croatian constituent unit." And item two says, "South of Mostar, the Croatian side considers the entire area delineated in 1939 to be within the Croatian constituent unit. The Serbian side considers the Neretva River to be the borderline." So items one and two reflect, if you like, an agreement to continue disagreeing; would you accept that?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know nothing of the context of this document, when was it taking place, where was it taking place, who signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You'll have to, of course, you'll have to accept simply for the purposes of this part of the discussion, that this is a document at Graz and that it reflects an agreement between the Serbs and the Croats. Are you aware of the agreement or is it a fact of which you are entirely ignorant?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of this particular agreement and I'm not prepared to speak on something I have no expertise upon.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I want you to look at paragraph three, please. "Both sides agree that in defining the borderline between the two constituent units in the areas of Kupres as well as Bosanska Posavina account should be taken of the compactness of areas and communications." Now this is your area of expertise. They're dealing there with the Posavina, are they not?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this is not dealing with my area of expertise. I see nothing sociological here. I see this as a matter for historians or people who are experts in documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, then what I want you to help me with is this: If it be the case, following an agreement of the type I've suggested is revealed here, if it be the case that following such an agreement, fighting stopped in the Posavina but continued on in Mostar where there was disagreement, doesn't that reflect top down control in respect of both sides, both sides to the agreement and both sides to the disagreement?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not necessarily. I'd have to know a lot more about the situation. I'm not prepared to make such judgements.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, then, finally on this point, if you have two areas, the Posavina and the Lasva Valley, in one of which there is a controlling figure and in one of which there is not. Would you expect, on your theory -- that is a controlling figure on the Croat side -- on your theory, where would you expect to find ethnic intolerance, in the one with no controlling figure or the one with a controlling figure?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would expect, based on what I know as a sociologist, for the ethnic intolerance to be where there is a firm majority of one ethnic group and a minority. Because of the general proposition found in the studies I've cited that where there is a great majority, it's the majority that tends to be intolerant, as in Slovenia and Kosovo which were found to be the most intolerant republics. So that works for the enclave as well and I cited the study in 1999 in "Social Forces" by Dusko Sekulic to that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But you really have no knowledge of the area and no knowledge of the details that I've been raising with you.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No knowledge upon which I can offer my expertise.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And do you accept that the Croats were in the minority in most of the territory of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What areas are you referring to as "Herceg-Bosna"?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm not going to take time on that. Can I have that exhibit back. Can I turn to something else, please. You quote Dr. Donia, and we can find it, if you want, at page ten of your report. You quote Dr. Donia from his book, "A Tradition of Trade" as saying, "At no time did Bosnians fight civil wars," my emphasis on the word civil, "along these or any other ethnic lines." Do you remember that quotation?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That comes from Dr. Donia's book written by Donia and Fine, and would you accept that that comes from a chapter written by Fine rather than by Donia?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no knowledge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, I can show you the copy of the introduction to the book if you want to have a look at it, lay it on the ELMO. I really don't think it needs to be -- just that page, two pages on the ELMO. Your Honour, I hope this won't need to become an exhibit, it can be if it's wanted to. What I'm showing you -- by showing it to you on the ELMO that the book is available. In the introduction to the book, there's page one of the introduction. If we go to the next sheet, you'll see that there is a reference to Chapters 1 to 4 dealing primarily with medieval and Ottoman periods written by John Fine. So that's where the quotation where you lay at Dr. Donia's door actually comes from. You've talked a lot about scholarship, what are you saying so that I can understand this? Are you saying that because he co-authored a book he should accept full responsibility for what his co-author writes?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a tricky case. I mean I've co-authored and co-edited books, and generally there is a degree of collaboration between the two and there should be some degree of mutual responsibility. This is a rather unusual thing to be doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we look at another exhibit, please, 2825, I think this is my penultimate exhibit. This is a passage from a book of yours edited by Cushman and yourself?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mmm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's a book in respect of which you said, I think, you had an almost perfect working relationship with your colleague Cushman; correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If you go to the second page which is -- and is in the introduction of the book something for which you share responsibility, just over half -- well, second paragraph, about eight lines down, we see this passage. "To be sure, Croatian offensives against Bosnian Muslims in 1993, particularly in the city of Mostar, were contemptible and indefensible; those events should be publicly exposed and those responsible punished. The International War Crimes Tribunal has indicted seven Croats including individuals directly and closely linked to Franjo Tudjman. Indictments of Bosnian Croats for war crimes is one indication that no side is without blemish in this conflict." A view to which you still cleave?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
