utterances.text: If we turn, please, to the next page, in fact the next page is 27 for context and it's really on 28 that I want your assistance, in the introduction to the book. And if we go over then to page 28, paragraph 9, just read this and see if you still stick to this, "The leader of the Bosnians, Alija Izetbegovic, is an Islamic fundamentalist."

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is a view we reject, of course, here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: "This is a variant of the more general orientalist theme rather than a comment on Izetbegovic's own book 'Islam Between East and West', in which Izetbegovic's admiration for the West is so great as to be pathetic given how the West has rejected him. In fact, Izetbegovic takes great pains to show the distinctive identities of Bosnian Muslims as being between east and west." And then this quote, or this line, "Anyone even faintly familiar with the history of Bosnia would find the assertion that Bosnians are Islamic fundamentalists preposterous given Bosnia's history of religious tolerance, pluralism and cosmopolitanism." Do you still stick with that?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Does that -- perhaps I should go on. "This frame is taken directly from Serbian propaganda, which uses a youthful work by Izetbegovic," and so on. Do you say that what you're saying there about the history of tolerance and pluralism and cosmopolitanism is entirely consistent with the report that you've presented to this Court?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I ask you to look, please, in your report at page 53. On page 53 at the foot of the page following an analysis, if we could go to the bottom of the page there's a man called Zimmerman who you deal with. The Court knows who he is, and you say this as a conclusion: "Thus, both Zimmerman and Donia assume a negative attitude toward any form of separatist nationalism and assume a positive attitude toward integrationist nationalism represented by Slobodan Milosevic and to a lesser extent Alija Izetbegovic." Do you really wish to say that about Mr. Zimmerman?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because in his book he very clearly singles out Franjo Tudjman as the nationalist, whereas he says that Slobodan Milosevic was not a nationalist but was simply bent upon power. So he, Mr. Zimmerman, places his more pejorative remarks for Tudjman. Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. I have -- the chronology that you set out between pages 45 and 48 and 49 of your report, 50, actually, was it your own chronology or was it simply copied from elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was copied from the Carnegie endowment, which I cite, their chronology.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I know that you cite it. Did you check it for accuracy before you included it in your report, or did you just put it in lock, stock, and barrel?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how well I may have checked it for accuracy.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think I'm going to leave comments on the chronology insofar as they're material for argument later, because I don't think it's going to use your time very usefully if I take time with it now. Would Your Honour just give me one minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There's only one other general point that I want to be sure I understand so that we can either lay it to rest or pursue it. When you speak of the clash of cultures and the differences that apply to Croatia, for example, do you partition up Croatia and say that it really does only apply to -- I beg your pardon. I'll start again. When you speak of the clash of cultures and the differences that apply to the former Yugoslavia, you really do, do you, partition up the former Yugoslavia and say that different standards should be applied to the Serbs from that which are applied to the Croats?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What kind of standards, Mr. Nice?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, when you were speaking, as we saw in page 2 of your report, which we looked at in detail, and when we looked at the passage about ordering food in restaurants and matters of that sort, do you say that those comments apply to all of the former Yugoslavia or only to Croatia or only to Bosnia? What's the position?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course there will be a complex continuum, where I think the United States, as I've indicated already, has a sort of fast-food orientation. There are McDonald's openings in Zagreb and Belgrade but not as many, of course, as there would be in Miami. It's a continuum.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just help me, because I'm not a sociologist, that you would understand; I don't pretend to be. In order to distinguish these two opposing cultures, advanced and less advanced, do we also have to look not just at where people come from, but at what they do?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I don't accept the premise of advanced or less advanced. I believe I answered that very clearly earlier on. I am not saying one is more advanced than the other; simply different.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: All right. On the concept of difference, do we have to look not just at where cultures come from, but at what they're doing at a particular time? For example, to build on your example of the train service and the restaurants and so on, do we have to look at what cultures are doing at particular times to judge their difference, one from another?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One has to look at a particular time, but one has to also look at development over time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Here we've got warring parties at some stage. Were it to have been the case that one party or the other was formerly wandering around the streets armed with sharp and dangerous knives and other weapons, would that be an indicator that they were different, and significantly different, from what you've described as "the West"?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, these are hypothetical sorts of questions. I mean, I really am at a loss how to answer them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You deal in theory and other people's research and you deal in the hypothetical, don't you?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Again, I stated clearly: I use very solid theory to interpret very specific events and works by others. Perhaps I can cut to the chase and say that in the case of Slobodan Milosevic, there was a certain degree of rational top-down planning in that, one can see that there was an ideology of Greater Serbia that had been present for a long time; that in 1986, Serb Academy of Arts and Sciences memorandum had established this as a platform; that there was preparation for war; that the Orthodox church did not oppose it. And so there, because the Serbs had inherited much of the machinery of the West in terms of having embassies and government centres, and even because Marxism, Leninism is itself a Western cultural product, we see more, again on a continuum, of a rational top-down system or planning. My point is that when one looks at the Croats, one sees a nationalism that is less prepared for war. They simply did not have, in 1990, the armies and the weapons that the JNA had. You had the Roman Catholic Church, which was much more independent of the government than was the situation in Serbia. You did not have anything like an equivalent of a Croatian Academy of Arts and Sciences that was making a programme like this. So there are differences, and that's the way I would answer your question as a sociologist, to look at mitigating factors and a matter of continuum, not these kind of black-and-white hypotheticals.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm not going to take that any further because, as His Honour Judge Bennouna said, we've gone through theory earlier today. 1472.8, please. This is my last exhibit. This is a review of your book "Habits of the Balkan Heart," and we can see, if we turn to the second sheet, the last page, I think, it's by Andrei Simic. You would accept he is a respected academic from the University of Southern California?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This is what he has to say. If we just lay it, top of the page, on the ELMO. Next page, please. Thank you very much. And it's just the top section, if we can get into that. "One of the most disturbing aspects of this book is its thinly veiled biases coupled with the intemperate use of judgmental buzz words. A blatant example of this is the description of the consumption of hard liquor at morning business meetings in former Yugoslavia is 'barbaric.' In a similar vein, after having established that the Croats and Slovenes are not really part of a Balkan culture, the authors hold that 'the Balkans exhibit more extremely the opposition between the barbaric and peaceful traits found all around the world.' . 'Habits of the Balkan Heart' cannot really be taken seriously as a piece of dispassionate or careful scholarship in spite of its reliance on a constellation of sociological and psychological classics. Rather, it constitutes a primer on the misuses of theory and data. Its principal value lies in its study as an example of political and national discourse transparently cloaked in scholarly regalia." And I'm going to have to suggest to you, Doctor, that that judgement on your book reflects very much what you've given us today in your -- and yesterday, in your report.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would respond that there are two very positive reviews of this book in the "Journal of Psychiatry and Law" and in "Contemporary Sociology." Yes, this is a negative review. This happens to authors. And I would also comment on the use of this word "barbaric," which is here taken out of context. I use it in the sense of Thorstein Veblen in his book "The Theory of the Leisure Class." In that sense, in my lectures I've discussed, for example, the bonfire at Texas A & M University legitimately as barbaric because it wastes trees. And, as you probably know from CNN, there was a horrific accident last year which killed 17 students at my university. And people have an emotional reaction to that word "barbaric," but I use it in a very strict sociological sense of wastefulness. I think that consumption of hard liquor at morning business, which is indeed very frequent in the former Yugoslavia, qualifies under Thorstein Veblen's theory. So this is a negative review, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Where I've asked you detailed questions about the facts, you have made it clear that you don't have knowledge of the facts and you have returned to theoretical positions because you are a theorist.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was very careful to say that I did not have the full context of the documents you put in front of me, and I, as a professional, I have to be very careful in giving my professional judgement.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Browning.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Dr. Mestrovic, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give it. You're free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just before Mr. Naumovski addresses the Court, the Court will have in mind that I raise the possibility of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. I was going to give a ruling on that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Whatever the Rules about cross-examination, it would appear that the Prosecution are probably right in their interpretation of the relevant Rule, that matters should have been put. There has, however, in this case been very much evidence, and we have to consider that in the light of the need to get on with the case. And as a result, the Trial Chamber has come to the conclusion that it has sufficient evidence, and we will not trouble the witnesses for more evidence on the topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm obliged, and I will respond -- or we will respond in due course, as perhaps suggested by His Honour Judge Robinson, by dealing with these issues, as perhaps with other issues, more by way of argument in due course than by extensive adduction or cross-examination of evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There will be the appropriate way to deal with it, and of course if the gentlemen want to withdraw, they can.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I just point out that actually Rule 90(H)(ii) was changed on November 30th, 1999, as I'm sure the Court is well aware. Rule 90(H)(ii) is the Rule that actually requires matters to be put to witnesses during the course of an examination. And Dr. Donia testified on July 16th of last year and Dr. Allcock on July 22nd, finishing up his testimony on September 13th. So the actual regime envisaged by Rule 90(H)(ii) after seven days, after November 30th, was not in effect at the time that these two expert witnesses testified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You don't want the witnesses to give evidence, do you?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Yes. Mr. Naumovski.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, our next witness is Dr. Petar Pavlovic, who is prepared to testify in public. However, since the Honourable Trial Chamber has already decided for this matter to be discussed in closed session, so let it be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, although I certainly will be in a position to deal with this witness immediately this afternoon, I've been entirely occupied with the experts up until this very minute, and the other steps I have to take in order to be able to deal with Dr. Pavlovic have yet to be taken by me. I forecast, from the little I know already, that it may not be necessary for the whole matter to be conducted, or any part of it, in private session. I will certainly need some time to discuss matters before I'll be able to make that concluded decision. May I, in the circumstances, ask for either an early break or an adjournment? We are, in any event, ahead of the Defence timetable for this week, which allocated all of yesterday and today, originally, for experts, and we will finish Dr. Pavlovic this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, what are you really asking us to do? If we have a quarter of an hour break, will you be ready then to cross-examine?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Quite possibly not, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It would be better if the whole evidence is heard in one piece.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I would respectfully agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We can adjourn now until 1.00. Yes, Mr. Naumovski.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I just wanted to help you with your decision. Actually, we have already informed the Honourable Court that one witness would not be able to come this week, as we had previously agreed upon. However, yesterday afternoon we realised that we had problems with yet another witness coming in. Something was wrong with his passport. He has to get a new passport. That means a visa as well. So we are afraid that as far as this week is concerned, we're going to lose this other witness as well. Unfortunately, there were circumstances beyond our control that were in place, so we could not really organise somebody else's coming in. So to put it mildly, we'll have quite a bit of free time this week, regrettably. So I wish to say that what the Prosecutor asked for just now, that is, to be given additional time for preparation, is quite acceptable for the Defence as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll adjourn now until 2.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.20 p.m. 2

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm grateful for the time. Mr. Cicak is here, and in the public gallery. There is no objection to this part of the evidence being heard so far as he is concerned in open court and I, indeed, would ask that it takes place in open court. If the time comes when the Chamber considers that it would be preferable for Mr. Cicak to withdraw, he can, of course, do so against the possibility of his giving evidence and the Chamber preferring him not to hear the cross-examination. But for the time being, I propose that he should stay in the public gallery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, very well. Let the witness be brought in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Doctor, please be so kind as to give your full name and surname to the court?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Petar Pavlovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Dr. Pavlovic, you signed on the 19th of January [as interpreted] this year a statement, an affidavit before the court in Vitez; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: There is a mistake. It says January in the transcript rather than May. We were talking about May, weren't we?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, May.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So the 19th of May. Please, Dr. Pavlovic, tell me, this sworn affidavit that you have signed before the court in Vitez, does it contain everything you know to the best of your knowledge and recollection?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: I fully agree with what I stated, with what I signed, and I -- that fully matches what I know about this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Along with this sworn affidavit of yours, there are some attached documents. Are these attached documents a faithful copy of the originals that were in the files of your institute?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I must admit that these are only copies but that they fully coincide with the original. These are special forms that are made by the institution for the evaluation of work ability attached to the retirement insurance company in Sarajevo. At that time, it was called the Community for Retirement and Disability Insurance of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It is part of the disability and retirement insurance, and it is the only professional organ that is entitled to give an assessment and opinion concerning an insured person whose work ability is to be evaluated.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Very well. I think that that is sufficient by way of introduction and, if necessary, you are going to give a wider explanation later. Dr. Pavlovic, the affidavit, the sworn affidavit that you gave, did you give it first and foremost as the long-time head of the Zenica office of this particular institution for the evaluation of work ability?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: I was chief of the institute for the evaluation of work ability for two big regions, the region of Zenica and the region of Doboj in which there were 20 municipalities. I can also say that I worked there for 15 years, that is to say, that I -- my experience is exceptionally good. I worked with very good people, and I believe that this assessment evaluation and opinion was given with the greatest possible degree of professional knowledge, professional attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Thank you. My last question, Dr. Pavlovic: You were not the personal doctor of Mr. Cicak, never; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: No, never. There are certain doctors, I mean every insured person was entitled to choose his or her own doctor. Certain work organisations had their own doctors that treated the persons employed in such organisations, so I personally was never this man's doctor. I knew this man just in passing from the street, it's not a big town. We would say hello to each other, but I never had anything to do with his medical care.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That would be all. Thank you Dr. Pavlovic. Your Honour this concludes the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Naumovski, do you wish to exhibit the two documents which were attached to the affidavit?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe that the witness has this affidavit along with the attached documents. I thought that he needed that if this would be necessary for the cross-examination so if the Court deems it necessary, we can handle it now, but then I would require another copy for myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, there ought to be a copy. If you want to make these records part of the court file, then you've got to exhibit them. Now, is that what you're applying to do with Exhibit A and Exhibit B?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely. Absolutely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Hand in, then, two copies, please. And we'll get a number for A and then a number for B.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document A will be number D281/1, and B will be number D282/1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Mikulicic, anything you want to ask about this?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. We have no questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you have your affidavit before you, Dr. Pavlovic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before we come to what's in your affidavit and some other matters, tell me, please, how -- tell me, please: When were you first contacted by lawyers representing Mr. Kordic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was in the second half of December last year.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the 27th of April of 1999, when Mr. Cicak was giving evidence, questions were being asked by Mr. Kordic's lawyers about you, so they knew something of your contact with Mr. Cicak. How did they know of your contact with Mr. Cicak? Can you help me?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know how they knew about my contact. I don't know what kind of contacts these are. But my relationship with Mr. Cicak dates back to the distant past. But this was just on very specific terms, saying hello to each other, that's all, if that's what you can call a relationship. But I mean it's not a contact by way of that kind of communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I only want to know, please -- I only want to know how, as you understand it, Kordic's lawyers were able to come and see you. What was their introduction to you?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, there are different ways of getting in touch with a person. I don't know exactly, but I do know that they called me to come to an office in Busovaca. That's where we first met. That's where we first saw each other. They presented the problem that had cropped up, and I said that there's no problem whatsoever and that I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Please pause. I don't want to know, and you mustn’t tell me, what passed between you and them. I only want to know if you know how they got to learn of you. For example, if it was a question of a friend of yours saying, "Why don't you go and see Dr. Pavlovic," then you can tell me, "Well, it was my friend, Mr. X or Mr. Y." Now, do you know how it was that they got to find your name? And if the answer is no, we'll move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: PETAR PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's not that I don't know. I think that my name is well-known generally speaking, not only in Zenica but also in Busovaca, where I work at present. Everybody knows me. So I don't know. Perhaps somewhere this question was raised, who was the chief at that time, or perhaps everybody said it was Dr. Pavlovic. So that's it. People know where I work and where I go, so there's no problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Are you still working at the same office or not?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: No. I now work at the health centre in Busovaca. Until 1995 I worked at the Institute for the Evaluation of Work Ability. And then, due to certain personal matters --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Please, by all means, if you feel you must expand an answer, do, but some of my questions will be capable of a yes/no answer or a very short answer. Who copied the documents that you have produced to this Court?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, with the assistance of the lawyers, most probably Mr. Mitko Naumovski, and the service, or rather the office in Busovaca. I think it was them. It was not me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So you personally had nothing to do with getting these documents; they were simply handed to you by the lawyers?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: They did not tell you from which individual, if they obtained them from an individual, they got them?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You therefore technically -- I'm not going to take really an issue on this, but you can't technically say whether they're genuine copies or not, can you?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: I can, on the basis of the correctness of the form, on the basis of the facsimile of the doctors who worked with me for 15 years, on the basis of signatures that cannot easily be forged, on the basis of the complete form, on the basis of the complete anamnesis. I can claim that the form is correct, or rather that the copy is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you accept that in your country, to take the medical records, for whatever purpose they're lodged, of an individual is a serious violation of that individual's rights?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: At any rate, any kind of information concerning the health of an insured person is not permissible. However, obtaining certain papers, I mean -- how should I put this? Perhaps I did not fully understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you accept that in your country, to take the medical records of an individual is a serious violation of that individual's rights, wherever those medical records may have been lodged, may have been kept?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Believe me, I don't know about this. I don't know what to say. Violation or non-violation, I know that in our country, medical files are kept by certain institutions. These medical files are sent from one person to another until finally a person obtains his insurance. So it is possible for quite a few people to get in touch with medical documents, but the question is the extent to which they understand medical language, medical terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And just yes or no to this, before signing your affidavit, the medical man though you are, you made no inquiry as to whether Mr. Cicak had consented to copies of his records being in the hands of the lawyers who spoke to you.

utterances.speaker: PETAR PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not ask and ...

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The lawyers haven't shown you, is this correct, any originals, they have only shown you copies?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: No. No, no originals.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I don't know if the Court has full affidavits before it, and if it does, if it has the registry page numbers legible in the top right-hand corner, they are on in handwriting, they are really the only way of really tracking one's way through the document because I want to ask, first of all, about the document. I don't know whether the witness will be able to find it, it's probably simply better if I take mine out. 14823 is the English translation and the original of that is 14809, and I'll take that out as well. It will probably be easier for Your Honour's colleagues if they don't have the affidavit before them, if the usher would be good enough. In fact, the original is all I need lay on the ELMO, 14809, and incidentally, I call for the original of this document to be produced to the Court, if that's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, you're looking at an original document, and those of us who don't speak your language are following it in an English version so forgive us taking some time. I'll find another version of mine for me to have look at. You say the documents you looked at are in order. This one, tell us about it, first of all, and then we'll see whether it's in order or not. What is it?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: These are discharge papers from a hospital, the Institute for Occupational Medicine, which is involved in curative and preventive medicine as far as occupational diseases are concerned. This is an institution which is not an ordinary hospital. It is a hospital for all examinations, not only for occupational diseases, but also for general diseases. This hospital, or rather this institution, the Zavod, catered to over 100.000 or 150.000 people; the population of Zenica and its immediate surroundings.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm going to stop you. We don't have all afternoon. You must focus on the questions, please. This document is the only document or copy document you have produced apart from the various actual retirement forms that purports to suggest that Mr. Cicak was ever treated for anything; would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So let's examine it together, because you tell us that the documents are all in order, Doctor. What dates was he treated as this form will reveal? Please look at the form, it's on the overhead projector beside you.

utterances.speaker: PETAR PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You're not looking at that document, you're looking at something else, will you please --

utterances.speaker: PETAR PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. On the monitor, it doesn't say the date or it's very illegible, but on the letter of discharge, because what you are showing me on the monitor now hardly means a thing, that is what I can tell you. It is the letter of discharge that is important. This is just a piece of information stating that somebody was treated in the certain institution. However, the letter of discharge says very nicely that the insured person was there from the 24th of January, 1984 and that a certain diagnosis was made, that is to say, this was 15 years ago. You will have to understand that I won't be able to remember absolutely everything, but will try to do something.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you explain to me please why the document that has been produced as a piece of raw material purporting to show that someone was treated in hospital is manifestly incomplete?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: I can say like many other documents, we can always find various shortcomings, however, in this letter of discharge, it says very nicely -- there's everything. He was observed not only for psychiatric reasons but also for eye treatment, internal medicine, psychology, everything that was possible at the time was used to see whether there was an illness or not. It says very nicely there. This is a very strong institution, a very good institution, exceptionally good. I don't see any mistakes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You are a general practitioner or some kind of specialist, please?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Specialist of occupational medicine for over 20 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But you have no experience of psychiatry?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: I do, and how, may I tell you straight away, that I worked -- perhaps this is not important, but I worked as a general practitioner, as a specialist of occupational medicine when evaluating work ability. I also worked in health protection where I worked as an advisor, and I worked on legislation related to these matters. From 1993 I was employed at the institute for evaluating work ability, I became the boss there. And may I tell you straight away that every doctor who comes to work at this institute for assessing work ability has to undergo certain course, has to attend a certain course for at least three months, that is to say, where we refresh some of our knowledge from psychiatry, internal medicine, surgery, eye illnesses, et cetera. This is a specialised institution that deals with assessing work ability. Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll stop you because I'm trying to get on. Would you look at paragraph 14 of your affidavit, please. This paragraph -- tell us, was your affidavit drafted for you by the lawyers, or was it all your own idea?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: This was recorded and it was presumably signed and I stand by what is written here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Whose idea was it to put in this paragraph a comment or commentary on the various documents that you've produced, was it your idea or was it the lawyer's idea?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't be sure. I think both mine and the lawyer's. The important thing was to bring here an accurate opinion about a letter and Mr. Cicak and answer any question that you may have about Mr. Cicak.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You were attempting to say in this paragraph that the diagnosis of syndroma paranoides would show bizarre behaviour and other symptoms, weren't you? You were trying to do damage to Mr. Cicak's testimony, correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: I don't really want to say whether I will damage or won't damage anyone. I'm sorry I have to say I am not an expert witness on psychiatry, but I, like any other psychiatrist, I can tell you what syndroma paranoides is. I know I'm quite competent to testify as expert about all the diseases which affect one's fitness to work. I do not say that I can testify as an expert about psychiatry cases here or elsewhere. All I can say that the diagnosis established by the expert team, and I was their boss at that time, all I can say is that they were correct. I can tell you that enough time has elapsed over course -- according to this documentation, I never treated Mr. Cicak nor saw him all this time, nor do I look at him now, but I -- his case history shows that for two years, he was treated, that all the possibilities of psychiatric treatment were exhausted after two years and after two years, naturally, under the disability law, he had to be sent to the medical board. I do not see that the physicians who were involved in this had made any omission. They were all excellent people, good ones. Unfortunately, one of them died, another one is still alive, but he is of a rather advanced age.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If this man was treated for two years, can you tell us, please, where we can find his medical notes, because such notes must have been kept and they must be available. Tell us where they are, please.

utterances.speaker: PETAR PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: I am not Mr. Cicak's physician, so I do not know what particular health unit he belonged to. I can't tell you that. He must have had a particular health centre where he had his medical card, and every time he would go there, they would put it on record what kind of treatment was prescribed for him and so on and so forth. Because you must know, these diseases are sometimes bad, sometimes good, but everybody knows what their outcome is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There is nothing to suggest in your file of papers that we've looked at so far that there was any communication from his treating doctor or his treating health centre, is there? Find me a reference, if you can, in the papers to the health centre that you must have referred to.

utterances.speaker: PETAR PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry. I didn't quite understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Of course, we're trying to approach this problem with our own perceptions of how doctors behave. But if somebody is going to be retired through ill health, on the grounds of long-term or substantial ill health, one would expect to find communication with the treating doctor or the treating health centre. And I'm asking you, please, in the papers you produce and say are entirely genuine, to point me to any place that shows where the treating centre or the general practitioner is. Maybe it's here, but just find it for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nice, together with this question, I'd like Dr. Pavlovic to explain what he means by what he stated earlier on in the transcript. He stated the following: [In English] "Sometimes bad, sometimes good, but everybody knows what their outcome is." [Interpretation] What did Dr. Pavlovic mean by that, that everybody knows what the outcome is, how they end?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: In psychiatric patients, one knows that they simply lose their fitness to work. That's what I meant. Nothing special. Psychiatric patients are under separate treatment, and if the treatment is good, then for a while they may be in a good condition and there is no distinction between a psychiatric patient and a healthy man. And at times a psychiatric patient, and one knows that, in their behaviour, in their manner of conversation and communication, can be very easily told apart from healthy people.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You don't have the slightest idea what you're talking about, have you?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: You're addressing me?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The witness, of course. I certainly wasn't addressing Your Honour. I was addressing the witness. I thought Your Honour had finished. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did understand that you're not turning to me, and just as well for you. You're not turning to me to say that. So I did understand you. Sorry, Mr. Nice, for interrupting. I just wanted, following this question, to ask Dr. Pavlovic if I had understood him properly. Could he confirm whether I got him right? So you're somehow rectifying what you just said, but you say that this type of disease, illness, can be treated, that you can return to normality, and that therefore it does not necessarily mean that you're no longer able to work or that you have to give up your work for good, forever. Did I understand you properly?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, quite. Some diseases may be brought back to some more normal state than before but never revert back to normal. I think you did understand my point. Perhaps I didn't express myself properly. But I think that psychiatric patients, as a rule, always move towards the worse and ever worse situation. Perhaps I may be putting it in oversimplified terms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Well, I must confess that I do not understand you well. Can psychiatric diseases be cured or treated, especially paranoia, which is nothing exceptional? Can they be treated or not?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Are you asking me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed, indeed.

utterances.speaker: PETAR PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Syndroma paranoides is something different from paranoia. And I should like to ask [as interpreted] you, I'm not a neuropsychiatrist and I did not treat Mr. Cicak, and I was not called to give expert testimony here. If I was, then that's a different matter. But then tell me. I came here to simply confirm certain documents which were shown me here, to say whether this was done by my institution, whether it was done by my physicians, whether this corresponds, the original, of which I was the boss. Because let me tell you, I never treated Mr. Dragutin [as interpreted], I never examined him at the time, nor is this my opinion. This was done by my physicians, who worked at the institute of which I was the boss.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Therefore, Dr. Pavlovic, can you explain to the Chamber what is to be understood by syndroma paranoides, which is stated as such in the document. We're not doctors either. You are a specialist. We're neither doctors, and therefore, a fortiori, not specialists either.

utterances.speaker: PETAR PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: I am not a specialist in that particular field, but a couple of minutes ago I said that we go through the training for all the diseases, or rather all the medical branches: neuropsychology, internal and all the rest. Syndroma paranoides is a set of syndromes. It is a multiple -- even the symptomatology is a multiple, from affective responses to impulsive responses, alienation, loss of concentration, loss of concentration at work, separation from the family, simply strange behaviour, strange behaviour of all patterns. That is what I, as a physician, can tell you, and I was involved in assessing one's fitness to work. As for the expert evidence, psychiatric, I do not think I am competent to do that today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: How do you think that your production of these documents is going to help us assess the evidence of a witness who gave evidence 15 years after this diagnosis?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, quite. I wonder myself, after 15 years, how can one say about an insuree or a patient -- that is, after all the time, how can I say now that he was such-and-such? Or if I already stated on one occasion that I never treated Mr. Cicak, nor followed him as a patient, nor do I have any insight into his medical card, which possibly records all his visits to the clinic and the therapy that he received. I see Mr. Cicak only on paper here, and in no other way at all. My assistance, that is, my help to bring this case to a close is all -- that is, the discharge from the hospital and everything that it says here, that is, the assessment, the findings, and the opinion of the disability commission, are 100 per cent accurate. That is, they are identical with the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You in fact know, Doctor, that you've come here actively to mislead this Court, because these documents are in reality not at all what they seem. And I'm just going to explain that in a little more detail. Between 1968 -- I beg your pardon, 1978 and 1984, or thereabouts, Mr. Cicak was, maybe as is his want, vocally critical of the communist party of which he was a member. Do you remember that? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: No. I'm not a man of politics, and I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. By 1984, Mr. Cicak, having been expelled from the party and been at certain forms of risks, needed to retire, or certainly wanted to, and it was well within the experience of your bureaucracies that retirement could be used as a way of freeing people from being where they otherwise were obliged to be and to work. This sort of medical discharge could be used as a ruse; correct? Something that happened not infrequently?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Are you saying it never happened, it happened sometimes, or that it happened frequently?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't know even though I was 15 years there. I am not susceptible to political games or anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I suggest you know perfectly well your wife and Mr. Cicak worked in the same department, I think.

utterances.speaker: PETAR PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did they know each other?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: I suppose so, through the spouses, yes. Well that's a small place, everybody knows everybody else, but it does not affect the commission anyway because then it wouldn't be a commission but something completely different, a private ...

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Go on. It may seem irrelevant, but you can confirm, as a matter of fact, that Mrs. Cicak is the maker of what were and may still be prized wall decorations, namely needle-point designs and pictures of one kind and another, correct, and that you have some of them probably on your walls; correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: No, that is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is it right that she does needle-point --

utterances.speaker: PETAR PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: No, believe me, no. I don't know. I did not see her for the past 10 years or so. I do see Mr. Cicak in the street from time to time, but it's -- we only greet one another.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It may be that you received both prints and money perhaps about a month's salary in order to provide and sign these documents. What do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: This is preposterous. I don't write these documents, nor may I sign these documents. What is important to us are findings. I can't understand that you are asking me such a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Would you go to page 14811, please, in the exhibits, the little writing on the top right-hand corner, 14811. No, it's not there, it's an original document. I'll lay mine on the ELMO. Now, you have examined these documents and you tell us that they are all entirely sensible and consistent and straightforward. Above Cicak's name, we see his wife's signature. Would you explain to me why? Who produced these documents?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: I am not sure. I am guessing now. Possibly Mr. Cicak did not take this, perhaps he was unaccountable at the time but I cannot affirm that. So it must have been why Mrs. Dubravka took this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Because the original of the document, which I can produce -- I am so sorry, did you want to say something?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: By statute -- no, no, no, I mean we do not have Mr. Cicak's signature here so it wasn't Mr. Cicak who picked up the finding but his wife because it is on the basis of these findings and the opinions. Certain rights, certain insurance rights derive for retirement or disability pension, and I believe that is why Mrs. Cicak took them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I don't wish to produce to the Court the original, but if you just look at the document that you've got in front of you which is the original, we can lay it on the ELMO, Mrs. Cicak's signature is certainly not there. So --

utterances.speaker: PETAR PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: No, if you compare it with the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you explain, please, how it can come about that these very important documents that relate to Mr. Cicak and his retirement are passed to his wife, unless, as I suggest to you, there was an exchange for money and indeed for prints, and you and your doctor colleagues were all involved.

utterances.speaker: PETAR PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you right away, I should like to ask you not to use those words because that is not true. As for the delivery of the document, it says clear here who it is delivered to, Mr. Dragutin Cicak, then the health institution, the physician on duty, the organisation that the man worked for, the health insurance community because the man was on a sick leave, and that's it. How did it come about that Mrs. Cicak received this finding and how it was signed, that is something I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May we now go back, please, to the question I asked you earlier. Can you find in the documents you've produced to us, any document that goes to show either where Mr. Cicak was being treated or even the name and address of his treating general practitioner or the medical centre where he was apparently treated for two years?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Believe me, I can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No. And are you really telling this Chamber that a major institution presided over by you dealing with the retirement of a person for ill health would neither send nor receive a communication from that man's treating doctor; is that really what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Let me explain it a little bit how one is sent to the disability board. An insuree is treated at the general practice clinic. If no results are obtained there, then that patient is sent to a higher institute, and that is the occupational medicine institute. They have the specialist services so there is a higher level of treatment. And if that doesn't produce any result, then that person is sent to the disability board which then gives its view about the person's work fitness. In addition to medical documentation, we also need the legal documentation or rather the job description of that particular insuree. So that we have medical documentation on the one hand, on the other hand, we have labour and legal documentation. Then, this insuree comes to us and we examine him head to foot while fully respecting every patient. So a patient stays an hour or two, sometimes more, sometimes less, depending on the diagnosis. The patient is examined and at the end of it, the patient goes out and then the council, the board stays here, like you are here, and then the chamber discusses whether that person is fit to work or not. And I have to repeat, I have two physicians on my board and from time to time -- on my council, and from time to time, we also bring in a psychologist. Since there is a psychological test, that everything that has to do with the medicine has been treated. He was with us, we examined him and, at the end, the chamber meets and decides on that person's fitness to work, ability to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. Just breaking it down into two parts. As a doctor, you will accept, won't you, just yes or no to this, that any person suffering mental ill health for a couple of years and being treated for it will have medical records going to show the treatment and the consultations that he has had; correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: That is what it should be, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And your last very long answer given to the Judges, not only showed a great knowledge of the law, as you say it to be, it also was a way of trying to avoid the need for your assessment to build on a general practitioner's records. I must suggest to you that's wholly unrealistic. No doctor would avoid turning to a general practitioner for help on a matter as serious as this.

utterances.speaker: PETAR PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: The board uses all the methods in order to obtain the best knowledge, the best information possible about the state of health of the person who comes to us. Why I'm telling you that, health cards, and then we visually look whether the person has had any case history, whether it was treated or not treated for diseases or not. I do not know whether this expert team used this or not, because one of the doctors who examined him and assessed him died, and I'm really sorry I have to say that, because we've known one another for 15 years, I'm sorry about that. So this doctor cannot tell you that himself. But we use all the methods like -- and again, I must compare it with you as you do it. So we use all the methods in order to establish one's true state of health. We have instructions. We have a manual.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Turn, please, to what is in the English in the pages of the affidavit 14820 and more materially 14819, and I'll find the original for the witness. I think it's all on 14806. I don't know if Your Honour has any of those pages. But if Your Honour's colleagues don't, I better put one on the ELMO if not. And I'll make the original available for the witness to look at. While they are coming to you, I should tell you, Doctor, that I've had these notes considered by a Dutch psychiatrist. Unfortunately he's gone on holiday, and unfortunately he has locked his report away before it was faxed to me so I can only give you a summary of what I understand he will explain to us if it ever becomes necessary. The Chamber will see on -- absolutely at the foot of page 120, can you lay, literally, the foot of 120 on the ELMO for His Honour's colleagues. Your Honour, give me a minute. Just to look at it, the first page simply shows that at this part of the report, we reach at the bottom of the page the findings of the psychologist. So now if we can go to the next page, please, because it's not headed we start at the top so what we're looking at here in English, and I hope you have there in the original is, first, the findings of the psychologist and then the findings of the neuropsychiatrist. Let's just see what they say, shall we? The first psychologist apparently says, "Emotional tension which influences general neurosis. Differential neurotic stages in the level of concentration." It deals with memory and as far as personality is concerned, "a general neurosis is expressed with presence of hypersensitive anxietal and partially obsessive, compulsive and depressive tendencies. On the basis of diagnosed abilities shows a change of personality." Then we come to the findings of the neuropsychiatrist. He apparently finds for the same patient on information gathered from wife and co-workers to which I will return, a clinical picture after testing and a psychiatric examination of paranoid syndrome as was previously found and treated. Never hospitalised because never wanted to accept something like that, but took medication. It sets out the medication. Incidentally, one of those medications is quite dangerous, isn't it, and would have to be the subject of a prescription, would you accept that? Nozinan, do you accept that it's quite dangerous?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Moditen and Nozinan and also this intramuscular Moditen injection that is given for one month, yes, all of these medicines require prescription. I don't know whether that time or all of these medications required prescription, but now all of these Depo Moditen and Nozinan require prescriptions, and there is strict control over who takes it, how, why, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: He goes on, the psychiatrist, the neuropsychiatrist, "...because of the illness and rigid attitude within his illness to treatment by a psychiatrist and institution, we are of the opinion that he shouldn't work. Syndroma paranoides." Now, do you know whether one way or another whether the conclusions of the psychiatrist are consistent with those of the psychologist or whether they are incompatible?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, right now I would not go into the entire problem as far as evaluation is concerned. I am an individual. This conclusion is relevant. The Institute for Occupational Medicine is a highly specialised institution, and it has a very high standing and it involves professionals of all kinds. It is their duty to give recommendations and conclusions regarding work ability. That is their opinion. We on the commission can accept it, but we don't have to.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm going back to my question, but I'll recast it. In a document which makes a total of sort of five different symptoms, you have the psychologist talking of neurotic symptoms and the psychiatrist talking of paranoid symptoms. Incompatible, simply borrowed from somebody else's records, Doctor, and you know it.

utterances.speaker: PETAR PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: A psychologist looks at things from a psychologist's point of view and a neuropsychiatrist looks from a neuropsychiatrist's point of view, and the two should not collide with one another. Different expressions are used. A psychologist uses psychological terms; a neuropsychiatrist uses psychiatric terms. Not both use the same terms. A medical doctor has medical terminology. A lawyer has legal terminology. In medicine, neuropsychiatrists have neuropsychiatric vocabulary, but they all work towards a final diagnosis. I do apologise. I'm only looking at a piece of paper here, not a man, and I'm saying something about what has been written.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: My last question probably. I've taken long enough on this. It can be found on Your Honours' page 14825, and I'll try and find it in the original. And I'll hand my copy of 14825 for placing on the ELMO and I'll find the original for the witness, if I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This man was quite ill, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Different psychiatrists would describe this in different ways.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Why didn't he have to be followed up? We've got -- I can't find the original at the moment. The papers are confusing, but why didn't he have to be followed up?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: I believe that they did follow this for about two years. At least, that's what the papers say. People should be trusted. I must mention once again that I did not examine him, nor was I involved in the follow-up.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm going to show you the reference. Here it is. It's on 14812. If I can have it back. "Follow-up not necessary." There it is in your own document. Not followed up because there was nothing to follow up.

utterances.speaker: PETAR PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: When the loss of work ability is concerned, there is no need to have a follow-up. If our assessment is that he is not able to work anymore, not work at all, why would we, from the institute -- I mean, we are talking about that kind of follow-up, from the institute. As far as a neuropsychiatrist is concerned, that is different. He is still being followed by his own doctor or a service that he belongs to. However, as far as the institute is concerned, in terms of evaluating his work ability, and also in terms of the panel that assesses this is concerned, the commission, the panel doesn't have to re-evaluate this. In some countries, it is necessary after five years or so. However, in our country, the situation was such that it was not necessary to re-examine things or follow up. It is not the health condition that did not have to be followed up and monitored, et cetera; it is the findings of the commission that did not have to be looked at again.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: From four statements or affidavits, and in some cases, evidence has been produced by Mr. Kordic's lawyers that seek to confirm ill health. One is a person called Anto Stipac -- sorry. Only three others -- one is a person called Zoran Maric, and one is someone called Niko Grubesic. Do you know how they got the idea to allege, at least in their written form, if they didn't say it in evidence, ill health, and mental ill health in this man? Did you have anything to do with that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: No. I'm a doctor. I'm a physician. I'm telling you that once again. I'm not involved in politics. I know some people by sight only, but I was not told anything. Probably in contact with the insuree or -- I don't know -- perhaps some other way.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm not going to ask the questions that would be built on the premise of these being genuine records and their irrelevance medically, in any event, to activities later or to recollection 14 years later, because I don't need to in the circumstances. Just to give you an opportunity in case it arises later, I'm going to suggest to you, Doctor, that it's not just in relation to this case that you may have done things like this, but that you may have done it on many other occasions.

utterances.speaker: PETAR PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry that you have such an opinion. No way. Once again, I'm stating that at least I did not do anything dishonourable. I read this solemn declaration and I am responsible for everything I said. The medical documents that were presented to the Institute for Occupational Medicine are faithful copies, and I think that the institute worked fairly and honestly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's all I ask, Your Honour, although I repeat, for obvious reasons, I would like to see the best original that exists of the document that seeks to show the medical discharge that bears no dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Dr. Pavlovic, I think that because of the way in which you were examined, we have to put things into right order, so to speak, so I have only a few questions in this connection. This Exhibit A that you have, D188/1, as it was numbered today, that is the opinion and the finding of your institute that you were head of for 15 years; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Naumovski's microphone please be adjusted. The interpreters are having difficulty in hearing what he says.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: This was signed by the doctors that you already mentioned. These are doctors who work in the institute?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. These are doctors who were employed by the institute only. These are their only jobs.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Exhibit A is number D -- it is D281/1, so we want to correct the transcript. Right. So these are doctors who were permanently employed by the institute. One question related to your institute, another one as well. You have teams of experts who evaluate the work ability of a person for whom this is required; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: However, you do not treat people. Your institute, and I imagine things have not changed until the present day, does not have the ability to carry out full examinations and medical supervision and check-ups, et cetera, such as classical hospitals do; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: That's right. However, we have specialised doctors. For example, when there are head injuries, brain injuries, for example, when the CT was not performed, when magnetic resonance was not done, that is to say, all these methods that the institute could not have carried out, then we are ourselves required from our services to get these additional findings so that we would assess a person's working ability to the best of our ability. So we have all these possibilities made available to us. Actually, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Of course. I do apologise. Perhaps I should tell you that you should not answer my questions immediately, because my questions have to be interpreted into the official languages of the Tribunal, and we should try to facilitate the work of the interpreters. And I do apologise to them once again. So of course your institute has the possibility of asking for all the necessary examinations to be carried out, but it is not a hospital in the classical sense of the word, that has wards where all these check-ups are done; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: To put it briefly, we use all methods to objectivise a certain illness, bearing in mind the illnesses that may lead to a loss of work ability. That is to say that we use all methods. Even in the institute in Sarajevo, if we do not have super experts -- neurologists, internists, cardiologists, et cetera -- then we ask for an even higher instance, if necessary. If we have the relevant -- if we have the relevant documentation, if we have the right kind of documents, we don't require anything in addition to that. Then we -- I want to say this once again. We look at all the medical documents. We look at the patient as a patient. We interview the person and then we deliberate, just as deliberations are carried out over here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: I do apologise for having interrupted, but I believe that the Honourable Trial Chamber has heard quite a bit about this. However, as far as the last page of this document of yours is concerned, that is, concerning the assessment, the evaluation -- I'm talking about the institute, not you personally -- and it can be seen that it was addressed to seven different addressees; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And these documents, these findings, were invariably present.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: In my opinion, this means that this original, so to speak, was done at least in seven copies that were sent to different addresses; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: The Prosecutor showed you a copy which was, I assume, sent directly to Mr. Cicak.

utterances.speaker: PETAR PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This could have been obtained by anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: My question is the following: This copy, this copy that was sent to Mr. Cicak, it does not have the signature of Mrs. Dubravka Cicak, whereas the copy that was attached to your affidavit does have a signature. My question is the following: As far as the institute is concerned, I believe that you will agree with me, in the files in the institute, there is a single original where it says who it was given to, and then these people sign it, the people who received it; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Only the original remains in the institute; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. So that is the first set of documents. The other one is Exhibit B, that was attached to your affidavit, and it was marked D282/1. This set of documents was sent to your institute before you made your own findings and gave your own opinion; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is the procedure that is required.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: The Prosecutor asked you about the discharge papers, and quite a bit of time and words were spent on this. However, it is important, perhaps, to draw the attention of the Honourable Judges only to what it says here before the stamp itself. It says: "Attached letter of discharge." See, over here in the discharge papers, that is document B? It says: "Attached letter of discharge."

utterances.speaker: PETAR PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. This is it, the paper I'm showing you now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: In other words, discharge papers from a hospital is just a technical paper?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: It's just information.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: That's right. And this paper contains the expertise, the expert opinion; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Mr. Naumovski's examination, but I really must protest.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I concur with what my colleague says, but this is such an obvious question that I was dealing with. It is technically such an obvious issue. So I'll try to redefine myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Dr. Pavlovic, please, this letter of discharge was drawn up at the -- you said Cicak, not Zenica. Zenica is the correct word. That is the Zenica Steel Works Institution.

utterances.speaker: PETAR PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Oh, yes. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So this was signed by the doctors who are in that -- who worked in that institute, and their specialities are also mentioned here on page 3; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: You have already said this a few times to the Honourable Judges, but for the last time: These doctors whose names are mentioned here, and who looked through all the documents, who examined Mr. Cicak, they suggest, by way of a conclusion, that he be sent to the Commission for Disability Insurance in order to evaluate the work ability that he still has. My question is the following: As doctors, as physicians who have had insight into Mr. Cicak's full medical condition, they believe it is necessary to send him to the commission?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, it says here syndroma paranoides. That is to evaluate work ability it is necessary to have regular check-ups with neuropsychiatrists every three weeks. You see, they still suggest check-ups every three weeks. The possibility has been given for us to assess whether the insuree has lost his ability to work or whether there is some remaining work ability or whether he should be sent to do some other kind of work, that would be in keeping with the professional qualifications that he has.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Naumovski, you're now referring to what document in which it would be -- or the names of the doctors that have examined Mr. Cicak would be mentioned and those doctors would have sent a report to the Institute for Occupational Medicine. Which is that document, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, D282/1 that was admitted today, and it was called Exhibit B in relation to the affidavit of Dr. Pavlovic. This is a document that was drawn up by the Institute for Occupational Medicine of the Zenica Steel Works. That is a completely separate institution from the institution that Dr. Pavlovic worked in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you put it on the ELMO, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The last page, please. That is the document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the document we saw earlier on, that's the same document, isn't it, which was presented by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Exactly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That comes from another institute; is that so?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise, I'm waiting for the interpretation. Yes. That is another institute, and then on the basis of their documents, the institute where Dr. Pavlovic worked continued to work and ultimately made a decision, so these are completely different doctors. That is what I wish to highlight for the Court. However, I don't believe that there is any controversy involved there so we can continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Of course, Doctor, you already answered this. It was suggested to you by the Prosecutor that in your document, in the document of your institute it says, "Unnecessary to have further check-ups," but it says here that it is necessary to have regular check-ups with a neuropsychiatrist, and that is what is suggested by doctors; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: I'm saying this that from the point of view of the institute for assessing work ability. When we are presenting an evaluation of one's work ability, we are saying -- very often we say that that it's not necessary to have any follow up. For example if a man does not have an arm or a leg or whatever, why would there have to be further check-ups in this respect? So that is the way things are, but on the basis of our opinion, there are certain legal aspects involved. So we are just a professional authority that is supposed to give a medical professional opinion concerning the insuree, that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: The last question concerning this document that is on the ELMO right now. In these documents that you have the opportunity of seeing, is there anything unusual there? Is there anything inappropriate there? Is there anything that brings into question the correctness of this document of the Institute of Health of the Zenica Steel Works and you say that they were a very professional institution?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: I'm saying, once again, that the Institute for Occupational Medicine is an institution that is highly professional and that enjoys a very high reputation until the present day.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So there is no reason to doubt the correctness of the information in the letter that was sent to you, to your institute?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: All of this is quite right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Dr. Pavlovic, basically today you were told that you were bribed, you and your doctors at your institute?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Believe me, nothing was more difficult for me than that. I am not afraid of this. This is all fine. I am glad to have come here, but the only thing that pains me is that. I made this oath and I am saying it once again, that never ever did I accept anything in my life. You can ask other people about me also. Let people who know me speak about me. I should not speak about myself. I'm so sorry that it is this Court that is putting such questions. This really hurts a person, I mean, I'm really sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The questions are a matter for the Court, and the Prosecution are entitled to put their case to you. Now, Mr. Naumovski, is there anything more that you have?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. Thank you. Thank you, Dr. Pavlovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Pavlovic. You are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you too.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If I can just intervene, the Court will, of course, recall that Mr. Cicak was asked questions about retirement when he was here last year. He was also asked questions about a Mr. Pero Pavlovic but nothing was suggested about ill mental health or anything else of the kind that I've raised. The Court knows that he's here today. If the Court may think it would be assisted on this issue by hearing from him, I realise, of course, the various ways in which this can become a peripheral issue either medically or for the reason that I've advanced one way or the other and I'm anxious, of course, not to clutter the Court's mind or the transcript with material that has become or may become ultimately marginal. But he is here, and he can stay, he will be staying until tomorrow in any event. We understand that the Defence are a witness short, and if the Court will want to hear evidence from him, he's only too happy to give evidence straight away or tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, may I ask you what is the -- why do you suggest for the Court to listen again to Mr. Cicak? [In French] I'm going to speak French. What point do you want to make? What do you wish to achieve? What do you think Mr. Cicak can add to all the things we've just heard in relation to the issue of ill health, ill mental health?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If the Court wished to hear this particular issue that's been raised by the Defence dealt with in evidence by both sides, the Chamber -- and I'm, in a sense, I'm neutral on the topic. I'm anxious not to press the Chamber one way or the other, but I make it quite plain that both we and Mr. Cicak are entirely willing to give evidence. If I can diffidently remind you of how all this arose, it was never heralded in the cross-examination of Mr. Cicak that he was mentally unwell and that this could have, in any way, affected his evidence. There were some rather delphic questions asked about retirement and Pavlovic and there it was left.
