Then, when summaries, that is, first of all the short summaries, yes, and then the longer summaries emerged, we started hearing the suggestions that he was unwell mentally. Rather interestingly and curiously at the time, one or two of the witnesses departed significantly from any attribution of mental illness to a much lesser form of complaint about him which made one concerned about the summaries. But that was all detailed microargument given the scale of evidence in this case. Then Pavlovic's affidavit was advanced and it was clear from that affidavit that by a side wind or back door, which ever analogy is most appropriate, and describe via paragraph 14 there was now a positive effort to attack him so that in the closing arguments, the written briefs, we will find -- I don't think Mr. Naumovski wants to say, but -- so that we would find arguments which will say you can discount this man's evidence because of mental illness. That's what is going to be forthcoming. Therefore, we first of all decided simply not to trouble Mr. Cicak with all this and to try to eliminate the affidavit on the grounds of tangential or limited relevance. When we failed to do that, we had to take his instructions, not his instructions, but what his account was, and his account is how I have advanced it. And therefore, if the Chamber needs to resolve this issue as one of the many small issues in evidence, it should probably have the witness before it and he's available to do that, but I am a not pressing it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understand you properly, you want to ask Mr. Cicak in what conditions he went into retirement. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Naumovski.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you, Your Honours. All I wanted to say was our opposition to this Prosecution's suggestion. I believe this is the third time that while Mr. Kordic's Defence adduces his evidence, some rebuttal elements are being introduced. The Prosecutor will have the opportunity to produce every evidence that he wishes in rebuttal, but I see no reason to do this during our case, and if that was the idea, that is why Mr. Cicak appeared today, then I think it would have been the minimum of decorum not to have Mr. Cicak sitting in the gallery listening to this testimony. So we oppose this idea of having him testify in our case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, we've -- we have enough evidence on which we can decide the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I think it's about time to adjourn. Can I deal with one or two while they are in mind, administrative matters. We shall not be sitting on this case on the afternoon of the 19th of July. That has been already noted as a Chambers day and in fact on that afternoon we shall be hearing motions in another case. And that may also, although this isn't confirmed, it may also be the case that we shall not be sitting on this case on the morning of the 28th of July when, again, the motions in another case will have to be heard. That last date is not confirmed, the first date is. Tomorrow, if it's convenient, we need to be working on the calendar for the autumn and I would like to hear submissions from the parties on that, for instance, I note that if we start Mr. Cerkez's case as predicted two weeks before the recess, we should finish it by the 20th of October. I will be grateful, Mr. Mikulicic, if you would consider that proposition. I also have in mind that we should sit on the final round of this case, that is on the rebuttal case rejoinder case, and submissions for two weeks in December, the 4th and the 11th of December. I would be grateful for your assistance, because it's difficult in this Tribunal to fix matters because one has to do it so far ahead, and there is not the flexibility to which many of us are used to in domestic courts. Therefore, your assistance about those matters would be helpful tomorrow. And you've got two witnesses, Mr. Sayers or Mr. Naumovski?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: We have -- I think we have one witness who is ready to testify today, but if the Court wants to defer him until tomorrow that's perfectly acceptable and a second witness coming this afternoon who should also be available tomorrow and Thursday for the Court to hear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: How long do you anticipate those will be?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The first witness is Mr. Marusic, his direct examination we would anticipate as being 15 minutes, 15 to 20 minutes. And then the second witness is a former ECMM monitor, Mr. Garretson [phoen], specifically with reference to Bugojno, one of the municipalities that we informed you about in our opening statement that we would address. His testimony, Your Honour, I would think 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So we're going to run out tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I think we will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Sayers, no criticism at this stage because this sort of thing can happen, but obviously, we want to remain on target and we're going to lose two days.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, if I may just say to the Trial Chamber we do not anticipate that the loss of the two witnesses for this week is going to affect the estimate that we have given for the completion of our case in the least. We still adhere to our prediction of July 17th and it may be earlier in the week than later in the week of the 17th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll adjourn until tomorrow at half past nine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: at 3.45 p.m., to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 28th day of June, 2000, at 9.30 a.m.
